title: Six Years of Watching
subtitle: Active surveillance of a papillary carcinoma, and the day it ended
description: Reading a thyroid panel after a suspicious aspirate, choosing a needle for a posteriorly placed nodule, recognising when active surveillance has failed, preoperative requirements, ATA recurrence risk with an aggressive histological variant, and what follows a lobectomy.

steps.title: Step 1/6: The Panel After a Suspicious Aspirate
steps.scenario:
A 44-year-old woman is referred to your clinic with a right thyroid nodule found on a neck ultrasound. She has no compressive symptoms, no voice change, no radiation history and no family history of thyroid cancer.

Her thyroid panel:

    TSH, free T4, T3        all normal
    Anti-TPO antibody       40.2 IU/mL     (H)
    Thyroglobulin           > 300 ng/mL    (H)
    Anti-thyroglobulin      normal
    TSH receptor antibody   normal
steps.question: How do you read this panel?

options.text: (A) The normal TSH means the nodule is not autonomously functioning; nothing else here changes the plan
(B) A thyroglobulin above 300 ng/mL indicates a high tumor burden and argues for prompt surgery
(C) The raised anti-TPO points to thyroiditis and makes malignancy less likely
(D) The normal anti-thyroglobulin antibody means the thyroglobulin can be trusted as a tumor marker

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

TSH is the only test here that changes the pathway. Suppressed, it suggests an autonomously functioning nodule, rarely malignant, and leads to scintigraphy rather than a needle. Normal, as here, and the decision belongs to ultrasound and cytology. Free T4 and T3 grade dysfunction only once TSH is abnormal; the TSH receptor antibody matters only if it is suppressed.

Nothing on this panel diagnoses cancer. Only calcitonin can, for medullary carcinoma, and it was not ordered.

Why the others fail:
(B) Thyroglobulin comes from all follicular tissue and rises with gland volume, thyroiditis, even palpation. No threshold separates benign from malignant while the gland is in place.
(C) Anti-TPO establishes thyroiditis and predicts hypothyroidism after lobectomy, but does not lower the risk of a discrete suspicious nodule.
(D) Anti-Tg tells you whether the thyroglobulin can be believed, since it falsely lowers Tg in standard assays. A true value is still not a tumor marker.

Keypoint: TSH decides the pathway, the antibodies describe the gland, thyroglobulin means nothing until the gland is gone.

Reference: Haugen BR, Alexander EK, Bible KC, et al. Thyroid. 2016;26(1):1-133. doi:10.1089/thy.2015.0020.

steps.title: Step 2/6: Long Enough to Reach
steps.scenario:
You scan her yourself. The right lobe contains a 0.81 x 0.71 x 0.61 cm nodule: solid, markedly hypoechoic, ill-defined with an irregular boundary and an incomplete halo.

It sits against the posterior border of the lobe, deep to the bulk of the gland.

You aspirate it under your own ultrasound guidance.
steps.media:
Load image 1: Transverse ultrasound of the right lobe showing the nodule at the posterior border, unannotated. Caption: 'Right lobe, transverse.'
Load image 2: A 22 gauge and a 25 gauge needle side by side, showing the difference in length. Caption: 'Needle gauges.'
steps.question: Which needle do you use?

options.text: (A) 22 to 23 gauge
(B) 25 to 27 gauge
(C) 18 gauge core needle
(D) 20 gauge with continuous strong suction

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

Two requirements pull opposite ways. The needle must be fine, because blood is what makes an aspirate non-diagnostic. It must also be long enough to reach the back of the lobe, and the finest needles are the shortest.

Why the others fail:
(B) The usual choice for a superficial nodule. Here it stops short and returns normal thyroid.
(C) Core needle is for repeatedly non-diagnostic nodules or suspected lymphoma, and at the posterior border it heads toward the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
(D) Blood contamination comes from suction and bleeding, not from bore. Strong continuous suction ruins the specimen fastest.

Keypoint: depth sets the gauge, not suspicion.

Reference: Haugen BR, Alexander EK, Bible KC, et al. Thyroid. 2016;26(1):1-133. doi:10.1089/thy.2015.0020.

steps.title: Step 3/6: The Day Surveillance Ends
steps.scenario:
The cytology returns suspicious for papillary carcinoma.

You offer a right thyroidectomy with isthmusectomy. She declines, and chooses active surveillance with yearly ultrasound and thyroglobulin.

She has been scanned since 2019, the year before this aspirate:

    2019    0.51 x 0.63 x 0.58 cm      Tg      -
    2020    0.81 x 0.71 x 0.61 cm      Tg      -        aspirate
    2021    0.82 x 0.76 x 0.74 cm      Tg    131 ng/mL
    2023    0.96 x 0.84 x 0.82 cm      Tg    230 ng/mL
    2025    1.04 x 0.93 x 1.01 cm      Tg    185 ng/mL

The sonographic category has moved from 4B to 4C. On the current study the lesion abuts the posterior thyroid capsule.
steps.media: Load image: Side-by-side ultrasound, 2019 and 2025, matched plane and scale. Caption: 'Initial and current.'
steps.question: Which finding ends active surveillance?

options.text: (A) The maximal diameter has increased by more than 3 mm, and the lesion now abuts the posterior capsule
(B) Thyroglobulin has risen from 131 to 185 ng/mL
(C) The TI-RADS category has moved from 4B to 4C
(D) The tumor has passed 10 mm and is no longer a microcarcinoma

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

Progression under active surveillance is defined as a 3 mm increase in maximal diameter, or new nodal metastasis. Hers went from 6.3 to 10.4 mm. Separately, a lesion against the posterior capsule lies near the recurrent laryngeal nerve, one of the standard reasons a nodule is a poor surveillance candidate at all. Either finding alone would justify surgery.

Why the others fail:
(B) Thyroglobulin fluctuated without direction and is not a progression marker in an intact gland.
(C) Sonographic category reflects appearance, not growth.
(D) Size alone is not the trigger. The Kuma protocol continues surveillance to 13 mm if the patient prefers, because the growth definition is 3 mm on a 10 mm ceiling.

Keypoint: surveillance ends on measured growth or on location, not on a number that looks bigger.

Reference: Ito Y, Miyauchi A. Gland Surg. 2020;9(5):1663-1673. Ito Y, Miyauchi A. J Endocr Soc. 2023;7(7):bvad063.

steps.title: Step 4/6: Before Surgery
steps.scenario: She agrees to a right thyroidectomy with isthmusectomy. She has no voice complaint and no prior neck surgery.
steps.question: What do you arrange before the operation?

options.text: (A) Laryngoscopy to document vocal fold mobility, contrast-enhanced neck CT, and repeat thyroglobulin with anti-thyroglobulin antibody
(B) The same, but non-contrast CT, to avoid an iodine load before possible radioiodine
(C) Laryngoscopy only; cross-sectional imaging adds nothing once the ultrasound is complete
(D) Baseline calcium and parathyroid hormone, since hypoparathyroidism is the main risk of the procedure

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

The laryngoscopy is the part that belongs to us: a normal voice does not mean two mobile folds, and afterwards the question can no longer be answered. Contrast-enhanced imaging assesses extent and the nodal compartments, and a preoperative thyroglobulin with its antibody gives the baseline that later values are read against.

Why the others fail:
(B) The iodine concern is overstated. Contrast clears well before any radioiodine, and withholding it risks understaging the neck.
(C) Ultrasound cannot assess retrosternal extent or the relationship to airway and vessels.
(D) Hypoparathyroidism is uncommon after a unilateral procedure, and a baseline would not change the plan.

Keypoint: document the folds before you operate, because afterwards it is an argument rather than a record.

Reference: Haugen BR, Alexander EK, Bible KC, et al. Thyroid. 2016;26(1):1-133. doi:10.1089/thy.2015.0020.

steps.title: Step 5/6: Reading the Report
steps.scenario:
Final pathology:

    Papillary thyroid carcinoma, tall cell subtype, well differentiated
    Two foci, right lobe: 1.1 cm and 0.3 cm
    Extrathyroidal extension: not identified
    Vascular and lymphatic invasion: not identified
    Margin: tumor close to peripheral margin, less than 0.1 mm
    Lymph nodes: perithyroid 0/1, level VI 0/2
    pT1b(m) pN0
steps.media: Load image: Final pathology report, all patient and institutional identifiers redacted. Caption: 'Final histology.'
steps.question: Where does she fall in the ATA recurrence risk stratification?

options.text: (A) Intermediate risk, because of the tall cell subtype
(B) Low risk, because the tumor is intrathyroidal, node-negative and under 2 cm
(C) Intermediate risk, because the tumor is multifocal
(D) High risk, because the margin is less than 0.1 mm

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

Aggressive histological variants, tall cell among them, move an otherwise favorable tumor into the intermediate category. Every other line on this report reads low risk, which is exactly why the subtype line is the one that decides.

Why the others fail:
(B) True of every feature except the one that matters. Stopping before the histological type is the commonest way to get this wrong.
(C) Multifocality in an intrathyroidal, node-negative papillary carcinoma does not raise the category.
(D) A close but uninvolved margin is not high risk. That requires gross extrathyroidal extension, incomplete resection, distant metastasis or bulky nodal disease.

Keypoint: the subtype can outrank the size, the stage and the node count at once.

Reference: Ringel MD, Sosa JA, Baloch Z, et al. Thyroid. 2025;35(8):841-985.

steps.title: Step 6/6: What Happens Now
steps.scenario: She has had a right thyroidectomy with isthmusectomy. The left lobe is intact. She asks what happens next.
steps.question: What do you recommend?

options.text: (A) Discuss completion thyroidectomy, since the intermediate-risk features may warrant radioiodine and it cannot be given with a lobe in place
(B) Proceed to radioiodine ablation now
(C) Start levothyroxine and titrate to suppress TSH below 0.1 microIU/mL
(D) Annual ultrasound alone, since a lobectomy is definitive for any tumor under 2 cm

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

The conversation follows from the risk category. Intermediate risk raises the question of radioiodine, and radioiodine needs the whole gland gone, so completion thyroidectomy is the decision that comes first. It is a discussion, not a foregone conclusion.

Why the others fail:
(B) With a normal lobe in place the iodine goes to that lobe, and thyroglobulin surveillance stays uninterpretable.
(C) Suppression below 0.1 was abandoned for low and intermediate risk in 2015. The target is a TSH in the normal range; years of subclinical thyrotoxicosis cost bone and heart.
(D) The stage is favorable but the subtype is not, and lobectomy is not automatically definitive once an aggressive variant is on the report.

Keypoint: settle the extent of surgery before the adjuvant treatment, because one forecloses the other.

Reference: Ringel MD, Sosa JA, Baloch Z, et al. Thyroid. 2025;35(8):841-985.
